_notes: Diocese, brother priests, money, buildings, and the public, from the parochial vicar's side. Flags defined here: pv_dio_told_vfc_pastor (spoke to the vicar for clergy about the pastor), pv_dio_signed_statement / pv_dio_refused_statement (the chancery's statement of support), pv_dio_on_committee (Diocesan Building Commission; the trap of usefulness), pv_dio_crossed_bishop (took a loud public position against the bishop: tlm decree, immigration letter, or the association letter; assignment and succession content should read it), pv_dio_reported_drinker, pv_dio_soft_touch (always covers for brother priests), pv_dio_lunch_with_the_one_who_left, pv_dio_roof_replaced / pv_dio_roof_patched, pv_dio_boiler_nursed, pv_dio_diocesan_loan, pv_dio_campaign_face (a capital campaign built on him personally; a transfer event should read it), pv_dio_money_told_pastor / pv_dio_money_told_chancery / pv_dio_money_looked / pv_dio_money_ignored (how the missing money was handled; read by pv_dio_money_missing_returns), pv_dio_academic_rep, pv_dio_asked_pastor_predecessor (read by pv_dio_parishioner_asks_knew), pv_dio_trad_chaplain, pv_dio_prog_board, pv_dio_saw_map. Threads opened and resolved within this file: pv_dio_missing_money (pv_dio_money_missing -> pv_dio_money_missing_returns), pv_dio_predecessor (pv_dio_predecessor_allegation or pv_dio_list_published -> pv_dio_parishioner_asks_knew). Risks: pv_dio_vouched_for_accused. Flags read from elsewhere: new_bishop_during_seminary (engine/seminary.ts), affiliation:trad_fraternity / affiliation:prog_caucus (offers/seminary.json), summer:chancery, published, career:*, past:*, origin:*, tie:*, path:*, speaks_spanish. The schema has no condition on the bishop's own alignment, so 'loud and aligned with the bishop' is written on positions every bishop holds by office (implementing the Roman decree on the 1962 Missal; the conference's line on immigrants) and gated with alignment conditions on the choices.

events.title: The Annual Visit
events.body: Once a year the vicar for clergy drives out to see the men under five years ordained, and this week it is you. {@vicar_for_clergy} arrives at ten with a legal pad and a travel mug and sits in the rectory parlor, the one with the good chairs that nobody uses, while {@pastor} finds a reason to be at the school. He asks how you are sleeping. He asks whether you are taking your day off, and whether you have a spiritual director, and whether the pastor lets you preach, and whether there is anything you need. He asks how the pastor is. He asks it lightly, the way he asked about the day off, and writes something on the pad either way. You know what the pad is for. What you say in this room goes into a file that will be opened when they decide where to send you next, and what you say about {@pastor} goes into a different file, one that has been open for years. He has an hour. He is not unkind. He has done this in forty rectories and he knows what the good chairs mean.
events.flavorPrompt: A pleasant interview that is also an evaluation. The vicar is decent and tired; the parlor is the tell.

choices.label: Say it is going well, and mean most of it
choices.outcome: You give him the version that is true on most days. He nods and writes less than you expected. At the door he says {@pastor} is lucky, which you decide to take as a compliment to you rather than a remark about the pastor. The file gets a paragraph. The paragraph is fine. Fine is what most files say.

choices.label: Tell him the true thing about {@pastor}
choices.outcome: You say it carefully and once. He does not react, which is how you know he has heard it before from someone else. He thanks you for your candor, a phrase that has a file of its own. Within a month {@pastor} is cooler at breakfast. Nobody told him. He has been a pastor long enough to read a vicar's visit from the vicar's face on the way out.

choices.label: Ask him, plainly, how long a man waits in this diocese to be made pastor
choices.outcome: He tells you: it depends, and then a number, and then the exceptions. He is not offended. He does write it down. You learn something useful about {diocese}, and the file learns something about you, which is that you asked in your first years, and the word for that in the chancery is not ambitious. It is early.

choices.label: Talk about the parish, not yourself, and give him a list
choices.outcome: You have it typed: the boiler contract, the sacramental records backlog, the two ministries that share a closet and hate each other. He reads it twice and asks whether he can keep it. He can. You have been useful, and the chancery remembers useful men with a particular fondness that is not quite the same as wanting to promote them.

events.title: The Dinner After Confirmation
events.body: Confirmation is on a Tuesday evening: eighty-four candidates, their sponsors, a church that is warm by the second reading and hot by the anointing. {@bishop} confirms them one at a time with the patience of a man who has done this in every parish in {diocese} and will do it in the next one on Thursday. His master of ceremonies runs the sanctuary like a rail yard. You hold the chrism and say the names into his ear. Afterward there is the dinner in the rectory, which {@pastor} has been planning for a month: the bishop, his priest-secretary, the pastor, and you, at the dining room table with the good plates. The pastor talks about the school. The bishop asks about the school. Then, somewhere between the fish and the coffee, he turns and asks you what you make of the place. It is a real question. {@pastor} is at the end of the table with his hands around his cup. The secretary has stopped eating. You have perhaps a minute before the bishop's attention moves on, and you are aware that a minute of a bishop's attention is a thing that vicars trade stories about.
events.flavorPrompt: A rectory dinner with the bishop; the vicar is asked a question he was not supposed to be asked. Keep the pastor visible at the end of the table.

choices.label: Give him two sentences and turn it back to {@pastor}
choices.outcome: You say one true thing about the parish and one grateful thing about the pastor, and you mean both. The bishop follows the turn without apparent regret. {@pastor} talks for another ten minutes and is happier in the morning than you have seen him in weeks. The secretary writes nothing down. You do not know whether that is good.

choices.label: Answer him fully, because he asked
choices.outcome: You talk for four minutes about {parish}: what is working, what is not, what the people are like at the 7:30 versus the noon. The bishop laughs once and asks a follow-up. The secretary writes something. {@pastor} clears the plates himself. At the deanery next month a priest you barely know says he heard you had a nice dinner, and it is not a compliment.

choices.label: Tell him one true thing about the parish he will not want to hear
choices.outcome: You say it plainly and briefly: the thing the chancery's numbers do not show. The bishop does not answer; he looks at you for a moment and then at his coffee. The secretary writes it down. {@pastor} is quiet in the car park while the bishop leaves, and then says, not warmly, that you have nerve. You do. It is unclear yet whether it was worth spending here.

choices.label: Answer briefly and ask him about his own first parish
choices.outcome: He is surprised to be asked and then he tells you, at some length, about a pastor in a river town forty years ago who did not speak to him for a month. The secretary relaxes. {@pastor} laughs in the right places. The bishop leaves later than his schedule allowed, and at the door he uses your first name, which the secretary notices.

events.title: A Memo With a Signature Line
events.body: It comes from the chancellor's office on letterhead, addressed to all priests of {diocese}: a Statement of Communion and Support for the bishop's pastoral plan, two paragraphs long, to be signed and returned by the fifteenth. The signatures will be printed in the diocesan paper the following month under the heading The Priests of the Diocese. The paragraphs are inoffensive. That is what is wrong with them. Nobody who reads the list will be reading for who signed; they will be reading for who did not, and the list will be short enough to count. {@pastor} signs his at the kitchen table without reading it and pushes the pen across to you. He says it is a loyalty test and that the correct answer to a loyalty test is yes, and that any priest who thinks otherwise is under thirty-five. You are under thirty-five, or near enough. The memo does not say what happens to a man who does not sign, because a memo does not have to.
events.flavorPrompt: A small loyalty test arrives on letterhead. The pastor's cynicism is practical, not bitter.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.outcome: Your name appears in the paper in a column of names, in alphabetical order, in a typeface too small to read without effort. Nobody remarks on it. That is the point of signing: it is the absence of a remark. {@pastor} says nothing, which from him is approval.

choices.label: Sign it, and send the chancellor a private letter about what the plan does not say
choices.outcome: You sign. You also write two pages, courteous and specific, about the gaps: the parishes the plan does not mention and the money it assumes. {@chancellor} replies in a week, by hand, and thanks you for reading it. Your name is in the column with everyone else's. Your letter is in a drawer, and the chancellor knows which drawer.

choices.label: Do not sign, and do not explain
choices.outcome: The column runs. Your name is not in it. Three priests you respect notice, and one of them calls to say so; two priests you do not respect also notice. The chancery notices in the way it notices everything, silently and permanently. {@pastor} says, over eggs, that he hopes you enjoyed that, because you will be paying for it in small ways for years.

choices.label: Ask the dean to put it on the deanery agenda before anyone signs
choices.outcome: The dean agrees, which surprises you, and the deanery spends forty minutes on it, which surprises everyone. Four pastors decide to sign together with a covering letter. Your name is on the letter. The chancellor receives it with the courtesy due to a group and the irritation due to its author, and the priests of the deanery remember who got them talking.

events.title: The Survey of the Presbyterate
events.body: The envelope is thick and the cover letter says anonymous twice. Inside is a survey of the priests of {diocese}: forty-one questions about morale, workload, fraternity, the quality of communication from the chancery, and satisfaction with your current assignment, each on a scale of one to five, with a comment box at the end that is larger than it needs to be. A consulting firm is running it. The return envelope has a printed code in the corner that the letter describes as a tracking number for response rates. {@pastor} filled his in over lunch in eleven minutes and says the last one, six years ago, produced a report, a committee, and a second survey. The questions about your assignment are precise. One asks whether you feel supported by your pastor. One asks whether you would recommend the diocese to a man considering the priesthood. You sit with it on a Thursday evening with the television on in the next room and think about who reads the comment box, and whether anonymous is a thing that exists in a diocese with a hundred and ten priests.
events.flavorPrompt: A well-meant survey in a small institution. The tracking code in the corner does most of the work.

choices.label: Fill it in with fours
choices.outcome: Fours, mostly, with a three where a four would be a lie and a five for the question about liking the people. The comment box you leave blank. It takes fourteen minutes. The report, when it comes out in the spring, says the priests of {diocese} are broadly satisfied and would like better communication, which everyone already knew.

choices.label: Answer every question honestly and use the comment box
choices.outcome: You write a page in the box, dated, in your own hand, about the things nobody says at the deanery. You seal it and post it and feel better for a day. The report, when it comes, quotes one sentence of yours anonymously, and two priests recognize it. You cannot tell whether the chancery did.

choices.label: Use the comment box to describe, exactly, what it is like to work for {@pastor}
choices.outcome: You are specific. You are fair, which is worse for him than unfair would have been. The consulting firm files it; the chancery reads the filed ones. Nothing happens for eight months, and then the vicar for clergy's annual visit is longer than usual and he asks about the pastor by name, and you understand that the code in the corner did what codes do.

choices.label: Put it in the recycling
choices.outcome: A reminder arrives in three weeks addressed to you by name, which settles the question of anonymity. You ignore that too. The response rate for priests under five years ordained is reported as disappointing, and someone at the chancery has a list of who disappointed them.

events.title: Appeal Weekend
events.body: The diocesan appeal has a goal, and the goal has been divided among the parishes by a formula nobody outside the finance office has seen, and {parish}'s share arrives in a folder with a video, a poster, pledge cards, and a script for the homily. Whatever the parish does not raise, it owes; the shortfall is assessed against the general account in the spring. {@pastor} hands you the folder on Tuesday and says you are preaching all the Masses this weekend because the people like you and because he has done it eleven years running and cannot do it again with a straight face. The video is four minutes long and shows the bishop with seminarians, retired priests, and a food pantry. The script asks you to say that every gift matters and to name the parish goal aloud. The people at the 7:30 give what they give and resent being asked. The people at the noon Mass ask, every year, what the money is for, and the honest answer is that some of it is for the food pantry and some of it is for the chancery's insurance premiums, and the script does not distinguish.
events.flavorPrompt: The annual appeal from the vicar's side of the pulpit: a script, a video, a quota with teeth.

choices.label: Preach it as well as you can, script and all
choices.outcome: You do not use the script. You tell them about the retired priest you visited in the diocesan home and what the appeal paid for there, and you name the goal once, without apology. The parish makes it for the first time in four years. The finance office sends {@pastor} a letter. He shows it to you and does not say thank you, but he does not need to.

choices.label: Read the script, show the video, and get on with the Gospel
choices.outcome: You do what the folder asks and no more. The parish comes in short, as it has for four years, and the shortfall goes on the spring statement where {@pastor} will look at it and sigh. The chancery does not blame vicars for appeal results. It does keep them.

choices.label: Tell them, from the pulpit, exactly where the money goes
choices.outcome: You have read the diocesan financial report, and you tell them: this much to the seminary, this much to the pantry, this much to the premiums and the chancery salaries. The noon Mass gives more than it has in years. The 7:30 gives less. A copy of your homily reaches the finance office by Wednesday, and {@vicar_general} is reported to have called it unhelpful.

choices.label: Preach the Gospel, and work the pledge cards at the doors afterward yourself
choices.outcome: You keep the homily for the readings and stand at the doors after every Mass with the cards and a pen, and you know most of the names. It is slower and it works. The parish comes within a few thousand of the goal. The people feel asked by a person rather than a video, and {@secretary} says the cards have never come back so complete.

events.title: Forty Miles on Christmas Eve
events.body: The vicar for clergy calls on the twenty-second at a quarter to five, which is not an hour at which good news arrives. A pastor forty miles out has gone into hospital with his heart, the parish has no vicar, and there is nobody else. Could you take their Vigil at four and their Midnight, and be back at {parish} for your own morning Masses? {@vicar_for_clergy} does not say the diocese would be grateful. He says the people out there have not had a priest at Christmas since the last one died, and that he has already tried three retired men, and that one of them said he would if you would not. {@pastor} is in the next room with the confirmation lists and has heard your side of the call. It is the busiest week of the year here too. The Vigil at {parish} is the one the families come to; you were going to preach it. Forty miles each way, twice, on winter roads, with a Mass at each end. He is waiting on the line.
events.flavorPrompt: A last-minute request from the chancery at the worst possible time. The vicar for clergy is honest about it.

choices.label: Say yes and drive
choices.outcome: You preach at their Vigil to sixty people in coats, and at their Midnight to a hundred, and you are back on the road at half past one with the heater failing. You say the eight o'clock at {parish} on no sleep and the people notice and do not mind. The vicar for clergy sends a note by hand. The priests who hear of it remember it longer than the chancery does.

choices.label: Say yes if {@pastor} will take your Vigil here
choices.outcome: You put the phone against your chest and ask him, and he says of course, and he means it, and he takes the family Vigil that he has not preached in years. You drive out. Their Midnight is cold and full. In the morning at {parish} he says the Vigil went fine and that the children liked him, and he looks, briefly, ten years younger.

choices.label: Say you cannot leave {parish} on Christmas Eve
choices.outcome: You say it as gently as you can and he accepts it without argument, which is worse than argument. He finds someone; he always finds someone. You preach your Vigil and it is good. In January a retired priest you have never met mentions, at a funeral, that he did the Midnight out there on the twenty-fourth, and does not look at you when he says it.

choices.label: Say you cannot, and give him the name of a priest who can
choices.outcome: You know a man: a hospital chaplain two towns over who has no Christmas Masses and has said, more than once, that he misses them. You call him first, then call the vicar back with a solution rather than a refusal. It is what a chancery wants from a priest, and it is noted as such, though the man who drives forty miles is the one they will remember at Easter.

events.title: The Building Commission
events.body: The letter is from {@vicar_general} and it is flattering in the specific way that means someone has been reading your file. The Diocesan Building Commission has a vacancy for a priest under ten years ordained; it meets monthly at the chancery, reviews every parish project over a hundred thousand dollars, and has, he writes, been told that you are the sort of man who reads a contract. It is true. It is also true that the commission has nine members, that three of them are pastors who have sat on it for two decades, and that no vicar who joined it has been made a pastor sooner for having done so. {@pastor} knows the commission. He says it is where the chancery keeps the priests it finds useful, and that useful is the most dangerous thing a young priest can be, because a bishop does not move a man who is solving his problems. He also says that a vicar who declines the vicar general gets a different kind of file. The letter asks for a reply within two weeks and uses the word honored.
events.flavorPrompt: The trap of usefulness, offered courteously. The pastor has seen it swallow better men.

choices.label: Accept
choices.outcome: You join. The meetings are long and you are good at them. Within a year you are the one they send the difficult files to. The chancery's regard for you is real and specific. So is the sense, when you look at the assignment list each June, that a man who reads contracts this well is exactly where they want him.

effects.key: Too useful on the Building Commission to move

choices.label: Accept, and make yourself indispensable
choices.outcome: You rewrite the commission's review checklist in your second month and the vicar general adopts it. Pastors start calling you before they call the chancery. You are, by any measure, one of the most valuable priests in {diocese}, and a valuable priest is a fixed asset. Two men from your class who could not read a bid to save their lives are made pastors before you.

effects.key: Too useful on the Building Commission to move

choices.label: Decline, politely, citing the parish
choices.outcome: You write that {parish} needs you more than the commission does in these years, which is true and which the vicar general reads as a young man who does not understand how the diocese works. The vacancy is filled by a classmate. The people at {parish} get their vicar on Tuesday evenings, and the chancery gets a note in a file that says declined, which is a word that keeps.

choices.label: Accept for one three-year term, in writing, and no more
choices.outcome: You know the statutes of the commission, which is more than the vicar general expected, and you accept for the single term the statutes provide. He is amused and agrees. You serve well and leave on schedule, and the chancery has had three years of your reading and a written reminder that you can count.

events.title: The Letter Everyone Was Waiting For
events.body: The new bishop was installed while you were still in the seminary, and for the first years the presbyterate has been reading him the way sailors read weather: from the appointments, the homilies, the men he has to lunch. Now the letter has come. It is twelve pages, addressed to the priests of {diocese}, and it is the first thing {@bishop} has written to you as a body. It announces a diocesan synodal process: listening sessions in every parish this year, a report to him by Pentecost, and a pastoral plan afterward that he says will not be written by the chancery. It asks each parish to name a coordinator. It uses the word accompaniment nine times; a priest at the deanery counted. Older men are reading it for what it means for the closures. Younger men are reading it for what it means for them. {@pastor} read it once, said that every new bishop has a process, and put it in the tray. It sits there. The parish has to name a coordinator by the end of the month, and you are the obvious person, and the letter has a tone that you either trust or do not.
events.flavorPrompt: A new bishop's first programmatic letter, read in a rectory by a man deciding how much of himself to invest in it.

choices.label: Volunteer to coordinate the listening sessions at {parish}
choices.outcome: You run four sessions in the hall. The people who come say what they have said for years, and some of them say it to a priest for the first time. Your report is read at the chancery because it is good. {@bishop} mentions {parish} in his summary. Some of the older priests note that you took the process seriously, and mean it as a warning.

choices.label: Write to him privately that you think the process is a distraction from the closures
choices.outcome: Two pages, respectful, direct: the parishes on the list need a decision more than a listening session. He replies in his own hand, a paragraph, disagreeing without heat. It is the only letter from a priest under five years ordained that he answers personally that month. You do not know whether that is a good sign.

choices.label: Do exactly what the letter asks and not one thing more
choices.outcome: {@dre} is named coordinator; two sessions are held; a report of a page and a half goes to the chancery on the last day. Nobody at {parish} is changed by it. Nobody at the chancery notices. {@pastor} says this is how a parish survives a process, and he has survived four.

choices.label: Say at the deanery that the process is theater and the closures are the point
choices.outcome: You say it at the table with the dean present, and three older priests nod, and one laughs, and the dean writes nothing down and does not need to. Within a month the phrase has reached the chancery attached to your name. You were not wrong. Being right about a new bishop's process, out loud, in his first years, is its own kind of assignment.

events.title: The Decree
events.body: The decree from {@bishop} implementing Rome's restrictions on the 1962 Missal takes effect on the first Sunday of the month. It goes about as far as Rome required and no farther: the older form permitted at two designated churches in {diocese}, neither of them a parish church, celebrants to apply in writing, no new communities. A copy is to be posted in every vestibule. The people who drove to the chapel across the river for the Latin Mass have read it already and some of them are at {parish} on Sunday, in the back, in mantillas, to see what the priests here will say. One of them waits for you after the noon Mass. He is courteous and he is not young, and he asks whether you will tell the parish, from the pulpit, what you think of the decree, because he has heard you are a priest who says what he thinks. {@pastor} has already told you what he thinks, which is that a vicar who preaches about a bishop's decree in either direction is a vicar who has forgotten what a vicar is for. The decree is on the bulletin board. Next Sunday is yours to preach.
events.flavorPrompt: The Latin Mass decree lands in a parish. A courteous petitioner, a pastor who wants silence, and a pulpit next Sunday.

choices.label: Preach the decree as the mind of the Church, and say that you agree with it
choices.outcome: You say it plainly: one Missal, one people, and a bishop who is doing what the Church asked of him. Someone records it on a phone. It reaches the chancery by Tuesday and {@bishop} by Wednesday. He sends a two-line note thanking you for your support. The man in the back does not return, and neither do the mantillas. You are, for the first time, a priest the chancery can point to.

choices.label: Preach obedience to the bishop without saying whether you agree
choices.outcome: You preach on the readings and, at the end, say that the decree is the bishop's to make and ours to keep, and that a parish is not a place where priests audit their bishop from the pulpit. It satisfies almost no one and offends almost no one. {@pastor} says it was the correct homily, which is not the same as a good one. The man in the back nods once and leaves.

choices.label: Say from the pulpit that the decree is a mistake
choices.outcome: You say it carefully, with the documents in your hand, and you say that a bishop can be obeyed and wrong at the same time. The video is online by supper. The vicar for clergy calls Monday; {@bishop} does not call at all, which is the point. Your name comes off a list you did not know you were on. The people who drove to the chapel across the river now drive to {parish}, and the traditional priests of {diocese} know your name, and so does everyone else.

effects.key: Publicly opposed the bishop's liturgical decree from the pulpit

choices.label: Preach the readings and say nothing about it anywhere
choices.outcome: You do not mention it. The man in the back waits after Mass a second week and then does not come again. {@pastor} is satisfied. Some of the parishioners who wanted a word from you, in either direction, file it as a thing you did not have. The chancery files nothing, which is what the pastor promised you.

events.title: The Pastoral Letter
events.body: The bishop's pastoral letter on immigrants is to be read at every Mass in {diocese} this weekend in place of the homily. It is four pages. It quotes Leviticus and Matthew and the bishops' conference, it names the enforcement actions in the county, and it says that the parishes of the diocese will not ask anyone's papers at the door. It does not say anything a bishop has not said before, but it says it in this county, this month, with the vans in the parking lots of two parishes, and everyone knows which two. {@pastor} will read it at the Masses he says and has left it to you whether you read it or preach it or both at yours. He says a letter read without comment is a letter, and a letter read with comment is a homily, and the parish will remember which it got. Some of the people at {parish} are the families the letter is about. Some are the families whose sons are in the sheriff's department. The letter is on the ambo in a folder. It is signed by {@bishop} in ink.
events.flavorPrompt: A bishop's letter on immigration read into a divided parish. The bishop's position is public; the vicar decides how loudly to stand with it.

choices.label: Read it, then preach it, in your own words and at full volume
choices.outcome: You read the letter and then you set it down and speak for six minutes about the parking lot at {parish} and who is afraid to park in it. Two families leave during the homily. Forty come up afterward. The chancery hears about it from three directions by Monday, and {@bishop} mentions {parish} the following week in a talk to the deans as a parish where the letter was preached and not merely read.

choices.label: Read it as written and sit down
choices.outcome: You read it well, which is a skill, and you do not add a word. The letter does what a letter does. The families it is about hear the bishop's voice through yours and are not sure whether they heard yours. The chancery counts {parish} among the parishes that complied, which is the largest category and the least remembered.

choices.label: Read it, then say that the bishop has confused politics with the Gospel
choices.outcome: You read the letter because you were told to, and then you say what you think of it, which is that it is a political document in a pastoral envelope. The sheriff's families applaud, which has never happened at {parish} and which {@pastor} says afterward is the worst sound a church can make. The chancery does not call. The next assignment list has your name on a line you would not have chosen, and the vicar for clergy is honest enough to tell you why.

effects.key: Publicly contradicted the bishop's pastoral letter from the pulpit

choices.label: Preach your own homily and tell {@pastor} there was not time for the letter
choices.outcome: There was time. The people at your Masses get a good homily on the readings and no letter, and the two who ask afterward are told it is in the bulletin. {@pastor} looks at you across the sacristy and does not argue. The chancery's compliance list has a gap where {parish} should be for the noon Mass, and someone asks him about it, and he does not lie for you.

events.title: The Deanery Meeting
events.body: The deanery meets on the second Tuesday at eleven in the rectory of whichever pastor lost the argument, and this month it is a rectory with a dining room that seats twelve and thirteen priests. The dean reads the chancery's items: safe environment renewals, the new marriage preparation policy, a reminder about the priests' retirement collection. A pastor of thirty years asks why the chancery sends a memo about the memo. A younger pastor says the new marriage policy requires six months and a weekend and that his people will drive to the next diocese. {@brother_priest} says nothing and eats. You are one of two vicars in the room and vicars in a deanery are furniture with opinions. Lunch is cold cuts and a decent soup. The conversation after the agenda is where the deanery actually happens: who is sick, who is drinking, who has asked for a move, which parish the chancery is looking at, and what {@pastor} said to the vicar general in March that everyone but you seems to know about.
events.flavorPrompt: The monthly deanery: bureaucratic agenda, real information at lunch. A vicar learning to listen.

choices.label: Eat the soup and listen
choices.outcome: You learn three things you did not know about {diocese} and one about {@pastor}, and nobody learns anything about you, which at a deanery is the correct exchange rate for a vicar. The dean nods at you on the way out. The soup was good.

choices.label: Speak up on the marriage policy: say what it will do at {parish}
choices.outcome: You say it well and briefly, with a number. Two pastors agree with you. The dean writes it down, which means it goes to the chancery attached to a name, and the name is a vicar's. The priests remember that you had something to say; the chancery remembers that a vicar had something to say about policy.

choices.label: Volunteer for the deanery's share of the retirement collection
choices.outcome: Someone had to, and it was going to be a vicar, and now it is you. It costs you a week of evenings and a great deal of correspondence with pastors who do not answer email. The dean tells the vicar for clergy you were helpful. The priests of the deanery learn that you will say yes, which is a thing priests remember.

choices.label: Ask {@brother_priest}, in the car park, what {@pastor} said in March
choices.outcome: He tells you, because you asked directly and because it is not a secret except from you. It explains several things about the rectory. He also says, kindly, that a vicar should hear these things from his pastor and that you might ask him. You do not. But you know now, and knowing changes how you sit at the breakfast table.

events.title: The Second Bottle
events.body: The deanery's Christmas dinner is at a restaurant with a private room, and {@brother_priest} has the seat by the door. He is a good priest with a parish that runs, and he is funny for the first hour and then he is something else. Nobody stops the waiter. Nobody ever does. At the end he drops his keys twice in the car park and laughs, and the pastor beside you looks at the ground. You have seen this before: at the seminary, at home, or in a mirror, depending on your life. What is different is that you are a priest of {diocese} now and this man is your brother in a sense the Church means literally, and there is a vicar for clergy whose job includes exactly this, and there is a whole presbyterate that has watched it for years and decided, each of them separately, that it was not theirs to say. He is standing by his car. He has a 7:00 a.m. Mass. The pastor beside you says, quietly, that somebody should drive him, and does not move.
events.flavorPrompt: A brother priest, drunk, in a car park after the deanery dinner. Every priest present has decided it is not his to say.

choices.label: Drive him home and say nothing to anyone
choices.outcome: You take his keys and he lets you. In the car he talks about his parish, and then about his mother, and then not at all. You leave the keys on his kitchen table and take a taxi back. In the morning he says the 7:00 and calls you at ten to say thanks, and neither of you says for what. You have joined the presbyterate in the way that counts and in the way that does not.

choices.label: Drive him home, and in the morning go back and say it to his face
choices.outcome: You sit in his kitchen at nine and say what you saw. He is angry for a minute and then he is not. You give him the number of the diocesan program and say you will drive him there too. He does not call it that week. He calls it in Lent. Nobody else in {diocese} knows you did this, and he will never forget that you did, and neither will you.

choices.label: Drive him home, and call {@vicar_for_clergy} on Monday
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy thanks you and says he has heard it before and could never act on rumor, and that a priest's direct account is different. Within a month {@brother_priest} is away on a program the diocese does not name. He comes back in the spring, sober and quiet, and he knows who called. So does the deanery. Some of them think you were right. All of them are more careful around you now.

choices.label: Let the pastor beside you handle it, and tell {@pastor} in the morning
choices.outcome: Someone drives him. You tell {@pastor} at breakfast and he says he knows, that everyone knows, and that the man has been carrying that parish alone for nine years and the diocese has not sent him a vicar. He says it as though it were an answer. You let it be one, this time, and you notice that you have learned how it is done.

events.title: Administrative Leave
events.body: The diocesan statement is two paragraphs and it is read at his parish on Sunday by the vicar general: {@brother_priest} has been placed on administrative leave pending the investigation of an allegation of misconduct involving a minor, dating from years ago; the diocese has notified the civil authorities; administrative leave is not a finding. It is in the paper on Monday with his photograph from the diocesan directory. You know him. Not well, but well enough: deanery meetings, a retreat, a funeral where he preached better than you would have. On Tuesday {@parishioner} stops you in the parking lot of {parish} and asks whether it is true, whether he did it, and whether you priests knew. The question has the particular anger of a person who has given money to the appeal every year. Other people are listening. The chancery's guidance to priests, sent by email at eleven on Sunday night, is to refer all questions to the communications office and to make no statement about the priest's character in either direction. You have been a priest of {diocese} for a short time and this man for a long time.
events.flavorPrompt: A brother priest on leave; a parishioner asking in a parking lot. The chancery's guidance is to say nothing. Serious and unsentimental.

choices.label: Say that the process exists for a reason and that you will not prejudge it either way
choices.outcome: You say it steadily, and you say that leave is not a finding and that the person who came forward deserves to be heard, and that so does he. {@parishioner} is not satisfied but he is not angry at you. The communications office would have approved the words. The priests would have preferred you had said something warmer about their brother. You said what was true.

choices.label: Say that he is a good priest and that this will come to nothing
choices.outcome: You say it because you believe it, and because he preached that funeral, and because a man is owed something by his brothers. {@parishioner} nods and repeats it to four people by evening. The priests of {diocese} hear that you stood up for him and remember it. If the finding goes the other way, they will also remember that you were in a parking lot saying it would not, and so will the people who heard you.

effects.value: Vouched publicly for a priest under investigation

choices.label: Say that you do not know, and that you are praying for everyone involved, starting with the person who came forward
choices.outcome: It is the sentence the chancery's email did not include and the one {@parishioner} was waiting for. He says, more quietly, that his cousin was one of them, at a parish in another state, in the eighties. You stand there for a while. The priests who hear what you said, and they do, note that you put the accuser first. Some of them think it was right. It was.

choices.label: Refer the question to the communications office, and call him that evening
choices.outcome: You give {@parishioner} the number and he does not use it. That night you call {@brother_priest} at the retreat house where the diocese has put him. He is surprised. Almost nobody has called. You do not ask him whether it is true and he does not tell you. The vicar for clergy learns you called, because the retreat house keeps a log, and says nothing, and writes something.

events.title: Could You Take Sunday
events.body: {@brother_priest} calls on Wednesday. He is going away again for the weekend, a wedding out of state or a conference or a friend from the seminary, the reason changes and the call does not, and he needs someone for his Saturday five and the Sunday nine-thirty. His own parish is twenty minutes from {parish}. He is a decent man and a good priest and this is the third time since Easter. He says it lightly. He says he would do the same for you, and he would, and he has not been asked to. {@pastor} would let you go; he has never refused a brother priest and says a diocese runs on the vicars who say yes. It would mean four Masses on Sunday, the last one at a parish where you do not know the people, and it would mean the youth group's retreat planning, which you promised, moved to a week you do not have. He is waiting. He is already, you can hear, packing.
events.flavorPrompt: A brother priest who asks a little too often. The vicar is learning where his yes ends.

choices.label: Say yes, and say it is the last time until he asks you for something else
choices.outcome: You say four Masses and preach the same homily at all of them, which at the fourth you notice yourself doing. His people are kind and one of them asks whether you are the new priest. He brings a bottle of something on Monday. It is a good bottle. You are, in the arithmetic of {diocese}, one favor ahead, and favors are the only currency priests actually use.

choices.label: Say yes, the way you always will
choices.outcome: You cover his weekend and the next one and the one after Labor Day. He tells other priests that you are reliable, which is the word they use. The youth group's retreat is planned by {@dre} without you. {@pastor} notices, and says nothing, and starts saying yes to the diocese on your behalf a little more freely than he did.

choices.label: Say no
choices.outcome: You say you cannot this weekend, which is true in the sense that you have chosen not to. He is gracious and slightly cool. He finds someone; the diocese is full of retired men who need the stipend. The next time your name comes up at a table where he is sitting, he is fair about you, and precise, and the word he uses is not reliable.

choices.label: Say yes, and ask him, since it is the third time, what is going on
choices.outcome: There is a pause on the line that tells you the answer is not a wedding. He says it is nothing, and then says it is his father, and then talks for twenty minutes. You take the Masses. He does not ask again for a long while, and when he does, he says why first. You have learned something about how priests of {diocese} say they need help, which is by asking for something else.

events.title: The Association's Letter
events.body: The priests' association of {diocese} is a voluntary body with a constitution, a modest treasury, and a membership of roughly half the presbyterate, weighted toward the men who remember when it mattered. It has drafted a letter to {@bishop} about the way the parish closures have been decided: no consultation with the presbyteral council, pastors informed by phone the day before the announcement, one parish told by a reporter. The letter is respectful. It is also going to be published, in the diocesan paper if the paper will run it and in the city paper if it will not, with the signatures of every priest who will sign. Twenty-eight have. {@brother_priest} brings it to the rectory on a Thursday and puts it on the table without a speech. He says the men who sign it will be remembered by the priests, and the men who do not will be remembered by the chancery, and that every priest in the diocese is deciding this week which memory he can live with. {@pastor} has not signed. He has not said why. The letter is two pages and the signature block is a third.
events.flavorPrompt: A presbyterate's open letter to its bishop. Every priest is choosing which institution's memory to live inside.

choices.label: Sign it
choices.outcome: Your name is the thirty-first, in a column, in the paper, under a headline the association did not write. The chancery reads the column with a pencil. The priests who signed nod to you at the next deanery in a way they had not before. {@bishop} receives the letter courteously and changes nothing about the closures and something about the phone calls.

choices.label: Sign it, and give the paper a statement of your own
choices.outcome: The paper runs the letter and, in a sidebar, your two paragraphs, which are sharper than the letter and have your photograph beside them. You are the youngest name in the column and the only one quoted. For a week you are the priest of {diocese} people mean when they say the priests. Then the assignment list comes out and you find out where a diocese puts a man it cannot fire and does not want seen.

effects.key: Publicly criticized the bishop's conduct in the press

choices.label: Do not sign, and tell {@brother_priest} you think the letter is right and the method is wrong
choices.outcome: He accepts it with a courtesy that costs him something. The column runs without you. Some of the older priests count the vicars who did not sign and draw a conclusion about the future of the presbyterate that is not flattering to you. The chancery counts the same names and draws a different one.

choices.label: Do not sign, and write {@bishop} yourself, privately, saying what the letter says
choices.outcome: You write it in your own words and it is better than the association's, because it is one man's. He replies, briefly, that he has read it and that he appreciates the form it took. The priests do not know you wrote it. The chancery knows exactly what you did, and it is the one thing a chancery respects in a young priest: a complaint it can answer without a reporter.

events.title: The First of the Class
events.body: The assignment list comes by email on a Friday in May and you read it standing in the sacristy. {@closest_classmate} has been named pastor: a real parish, a school, a town with a name. He is the first of your class. You were ordained on the same morning, kneeling on the same carpet, and you have compared notes ever since about pastors and rectories and the vicar for clergy's visits, and now there is a line between the two of you that a bishop drew. He calls before you can. He is embarrassed and elated and he wants you to say it is fine, and it is fine, and it is also the first time since ordination that you have done arithmetic about yourself. {@pastor} reads the list at lunch and says the parish is a hard one and that the chancery does not give the first pastorate to the best man, it gives it to the man it can spare. He may be right. He may be consoling you. The installation is in three weeks, and your classmate has asked you to come, and to sit in the front with the priests, and to be glad.
events.flavorPrompt: A classmate is made pastor first. The vicar's envy is precise and he is ashamed of it.

choices.label: Go to the installation, sit in the front, and stay for the reception
choices.outcome: You go. The dean installs him; he reads the profession of faith with a steady voice and you are, for most of the Mass, only glad. At the reception his mother finds you and says he talks about you constantly. You drive home late and the arithmetic is still there in the passenger seat, quieter. You did the thing a friend does, and it will be remembered by the one person who matters.

choices.label: Call {@vicar_for_clergy} and ask, carefully, what the chancery is waiting for from you
choices.outcome: He is honest, which is a courtesy and a warning. He tells you what the file says, in general terms, and what the bishop looks for, and that four years is not a long time. It is useful. It also goes into the file that you called, in the week your classmate was named, to ask about yourself, and that is how ambition looks from a desk.

choices.label: Congratulate him properly, and find a reason not to go
choices.outcome: There is a funeral, or there could be one. You send a card with a real sentence in it. He understands, or says he does. The priests who noticed your absence draw one of two conclusions and neither is generous. At night you find you are praying about it, which is at least the right direction to face.

choices.label: Go, and afterward ask him, honestly, what he did that you did not
choices.outcome: He tells you, at his new kitchen table, after the reception: the committee he served on, the pastor who wrote for him, the year he said yes to the chancery three times. He is not boasting. He is telling you how {diocese} works, because you asked and because you are his friend. You leave knowing more than the vicar for clergy would have told you, and it cost you only the asking.

events.title: The Second Floor
events.body: {@rival_classmate} has been appointed to the chancery: priest-secretary to the bishop, with an office on the second floor and a parking space with his name on it. It is the assignment every class has one man made for. The letter announcing it says he will assist with correspondence and scheduling, which means that every letter you write to {@bishop} will be opened by him and every request for an appointment will cross his desk, and that the vicar for clergy will, from now on, hear the news of the presbyterate from a man who knelt beside you at ordination and did not like you then. {@pastor} says the bishop's secretary is the least powerful man in the chancery and the best informed, and that the two facts make him dangerous only to people who give him something to know. At the next deanery two priests ask whether you and he were friends. You give the answer that is true. He sends a Christmas card to the rectory in December with a note that is perfectly correct.
events.flavorPrompt: The rival classmate becomes the bishop's secretary. Nothing has happened yet, and everything has changed.

choices.label: Write him a note of congratulations that means it
choices.outcome: You write four lines and one of them is generous in a way that costs you. He replies, formally, and then a month later he calls about a scheduling matter and stays on the line a minute longer than he needed to. It is not friendship. It is the beginning of a working arrangement, which in a chancery is worth more.

choices.label: Make sure nothing that crosses his desk from {parish} can be faulted
choices.outcome: Every faculty request, every sacramental record, every reply to a chancery memo from {parish} is on time and correct for the next year, and it is because of him. {@secretary} notices the change and asks whether the chancery has been complaining. It has not. It has no reason to, which was the point, and it costs you an evening a month.

choices.label: Say what you think of the appointment at the next class dinner
choices.outcome: You say it at the table, and it is funny, and three classmates laugh, and one of them repeats it at a deanery, and the deanery has a pastor whose brother is a canon lawyer at the chancery. It reaches the second floor in eleven days. He does not mention it. He never mentions it. Your next three letters to the bishop are answered promptly and late.

choices.label: Ask him for something small, so he knows you will
choices.outcome: You need twenty minutes with the bishop about the school and you call the second floor and ask for it as a classmate. He gives it to you in nine days, which is fast, and he sits in on the meeting, which is the price. You have established that the channel works. He has established that it runs through him.

events.title: The One Who Left
events.body: {@random_classmate} has left. You heard it at the deanery, the way you hear everything: a pastor said it between the soup and the coffee and the table went quiet and then moved on. Administrative leave, then a letter to the bishop, then nothing; the diocese does not announce a man who walks out. Now he is calling you. He is in a city three hours away and he has a job in a hospital's billing office and an apartment with a window, and he wants to know if you would come for lunch, or if that is not allowed, and he laughs when he says it, and the laugh is the same one from the seminary corridor. He was ordained the same day you were. He is not asking for absolution or argument. He wants to see somebody who knew him before. {@pastor} says, when you mention it, that the men who leave always call one classmate, and that it is a kind of honor to be the one, and a kind of risk, and that he had lunch with his once and never again. He does not say why.
events.flavorPrompt: A classmate who has left the priesthood calls. Written with respect for him and for the one who stayed.

choices.label: Drive the three hours and have lunch
choices.outcome: He looks well. He talks about the billing office and a woman he has met and he does not talk about the priesthood until the coffee, and then he says, not unkindly, that you should not stay in for him or for anyone. You drive home in the dark and say Compline aloud in the car, which you have not done in a year. He was your friend. He still is.

choices.label: Keep it to the phone, and keep calling
choices.outcome: You do not go. You call him on the first of the month for a year, and he answers most times, and it becomes a thing you both rely on without saying so. {@pastor} approves of the distance and does not know about the calls. It is a friendship kept in a drawer, which is where a good deal of a priest's life turns out to be kept.

choices.label: Tell him you cannot, and mean the cannot
choices.outcome: You tell him the truth: that you are not sure you could sit across from him without it costing you something you need this year. He is quiet and then he says he understands, and that he asked you because he thought you might say that. You do not hear from him again. The priests who know you did not go think it was the correct thing. It was a kind of correct.

choices.label: Go, and ask him what it is like on the other side
choices.outcome: He tells you. Not the freedom, which he says is overrated, but the quiet: nobody needs him at seven in the morning and he has not decided whether he can bear it. You listen for two hours. On the drive back you are not sure what you asked for or what you got. You know, now, what the door looks like from the far side, and it is a plain door.

events.title: His Mother
events.body: {@closest_classmate} calls at six in the morning, which is when priests call each other about death. His mother died in the night. He is at the house. He is, for the first time since you have known him, not able to finish a sentence, and what he asks is whether you would preach the funeral, because he will concelebrate and cannot get through a homily and does not want a stranger to do it. The funeral is Thursday, two hours away. It is a week in which {parish} has its own dead, a wedding on Saturday, and a pastor who has already said, twice, that the vicar is out of the building too much. You met her four times: at ordination, at a Christmas, at two dinners where she fed you like a son and asked whether the diocese was treating you both properly. He is waiting on the line. Behind him you can hear a kettle and a sibling talking to a funeral director.
events.flavorPrompt: A classmate's mother has died and he asks the player to preach. The week is full; the friendship is exact.

choices.label: Say yes, and write the homily tonight
choices.outcome: You write it at the kitchen table after the last appointment and it is about her hands, which you remember. On Thursday he concelebrates and weeps at the commendation and you keep going. Afterward his father holds your arm for a long time. You drive back for the wedding rehearsal and are late, and {@pastor} says nothing, because even he knows what Thursday was.

choices.label: Go and concelebrate, but tell him the pastor of her parish should preach
choices.outcome: He accepts it without argument; he is past arguing. Her pastor preaches, competently, about a woman he knew from the second pew. You stand at the altar with your classmate and hold him up at the commendation, and that is a thing too. He thanks you afterward. He wanted the other thing.

choices.label: Tell him you cannot leave {parish} in Holy Week
choices.outcome: It is Wednesday of Holy Week and the funeral is Holy Thursday morning, before the Mass of the Lord's Supper, and there is no way to be two hours away and back for the washing of feet. You tell him. He says he knows, that he should not have asked, and that he will ask his old spiritual director. You do the Triduum at {parish} well and think of her at every commendation for a year.

choices.label: Go anyway, and leave {@pastor} with Holy Thursday
choices.outcome: You preach her funeral on the morning of Holy Thursday two hours away and drive back with the chrism Mass oils still in the car. {@pastor} says the Mass of the Lord's Supper alone with a deacon and does not forgive you for a month. Your classmate will never forget it, and neither will the chancery, which hears from the pastor that the vicar was absent for the Triduum.

events.title: The Roof
events.body: The roof of {parish} has been patched every spring for a decade and the last patch has failed above the choir loft, where the water is now coming through the plaster in a stain the shape of a country. The roofer's estimate is on the rectory table: full replacement, slate to match, a number with three commas. {@maintenance} says the roofer is honest and the number is real. The finance council meets Tuesday. {@pastor} has told them about the roof every year for six years and they have voted every year for the patch, and he has decided, without asking you, that this year you will present it, because the council likes you and is tired of him. He hands you the estimate and the engineer's report and a folder of photographs and says to make them see it. You have been a priest for a short while and you are about to ask eleven laypeople for more money than the parish has, in someone else's parish, for a building you will not be in when the slate is paid for.
events.flavorPrompt: The vicar is sent to sell a roof to the finance council. A pastor's problem handed down.

choices.label: Present the full replacement, with the photographs, and ask for the loan
choices.outcome: You bring the photographs on a laptop and the engineer's paragraph about the trusses, and you say the sentence {@pastor} could not: that a patch this year is money thrown at the sky. They vote for the loan, seven to four. The deposit goes out in a week. The pastor says in the sacristy that he should have had you do it years ago, which is a compliment with a barb in it, since you were in seminary.

choices.label: Present the estimate, and then propose one more patch to get through the winter
choices.outcome: The council is relieved to be offered the thing they were going to do anyway. The patch goes on in October. {@maintenance} does not speak to you for a week, because he is the one who will be on the roof in March with a bucket. {@pastor} says you gave them an exit and that a priest who gives a finance council an exit will never get a roof.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} it is his roof and his council and he should present it
choices.outcome: He does, for the seventh year, and they vote for the patch, for the seventh year. He is cold at breakfast and you understand that he asked you because he had run out of ways to ask them. You were right that it was his to do. You were also the only new thing he had, and you declined to be used, which is a right a vicar has and a cost a vicar pays.

choices.label: Ask the council to fund an independent survey before they vote on anything
choices.outcome: You have read the engineer's report and noticed it was commissioned by the roofer. The council, which contains two lawyers, sees the point at once. The survey costs a little and takes a month, and it says the roofer was right, and now the council believes it, which they never did when the pastor said so. The loan vote comes in the spring and passes. {@pastor} is irritated and grateful in roughly equal measure.

events.title: The Boiler in Advent
events.body: The boiler at {parish} is older than {@pastor} and it fails on the first Sunday of Advent, at the 7:30, in the way boilers fail: a noise in the basement, then no noise, then the church cooling by a degree a minute while the lector reads Isaiah. The people keep their coats on. {@maintenance} gets it going by the noon Mass with a part he had been keeping in his truck for exactly this, and comes to the rectory afterward with his hands still black to say that it will not do that twice. Replacement is a number {@pastor} says the parish does not have in December; the Christmas collection is three weeks away and already spoken for. {@maintenance} says he can keep it alive until Easter if nobody asks him how. The pastor is looking at you, because the vicar is the one who says the early Mass, and because the basement is where he sends people he does not want to decide things in front of. There are four Sundays of Advent and two Christmas Vigils and the temperature is going down.
events.flavorPrompt: A boiler dying in Advent. The maintenance man is the competent one; the money is not there.

choices.label: Push {@pastor} to replace it now, before Christmas, whatever it costs
choices.outcome: He agrees on the second Sunday, after the 7:30 is said in coats again. The new unit goes in the week before Christmas with the contractor working through a Saturday, and the Vigil is warm. The account is empty until Lent. {@secretary} moves two bills to January without telling anyone, and the people at the Vigil never know how close they came to hearing the Gospel in their breath.

choices.label: Let {@maintenance} nurse it through to Easter, and do not ask him how
choices.outcome: He does, with parts from a boiler at a closed parish and a Sunday morning ritual in the basement you learn not to interrupt. The church is cold at the 7:30 all winter and the people who come to the 7:30 are the ones who do not complain. In Lent it fails for good, and the replacement costs more in March than it would have in December, and everybody knew it would.

choices.label: Call the diocesan finance office and ask about an emergency loan
choices.outcome: There is a fund for exactly this and nobody at {parish} had asked. The paperwork takes nine days and {@pastor}'s signature, which he gives with the look of a man who has been shown something in his own house. The boiler is replaced before Gaudete Sunday. The loan sits on the books for five years with the assessment, and the finance office now knows the name of the vicar at {parish}.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to let you preach a second collection for it on Gaudete Sunday
choices.outcome: You preach on the boiler, which is not a thing you were taught to preach on, and you make them laugh in their coats and then you make the point. The second collection is the largest in the parish's memory that is not Christmas. It does not cover the unit. It covers enough that the pastor signs the contract. The Christmas collection is lighter than usual, and the pastor notices.

events.title: The Face of the Campaign
events.body: {@pastor} has hired a firm. The firm has done a feasibility study of {parish}, which cost more than you make in a year, and the study says the parish can raise a great deal of money for a building project if the campaign has the right face, and the study, in a paragraph the pastor shows you, says that face is yours. The people like you. They say so to the consultants, who write it down. The pastor is not offended; he is sixty and tired and relieved. He wants your photograph on the brochure and your voice on the video and you at the podium at the kickoff dinner, and he wants it because it will work. It will work. It will also tie the largest financial undertaking of this parish in thirty years to a vicar who will be moved in two or three years by a chancery that does not consult brochures, and every pledge card will have, in the minds of the people who sign it, your name on the other side. The consultants have a timeline. The kickoff is in six weeks.
events.flavorPrompt: The charismatic vicar is asked to be the face of a campaign he will not be here to finish. Charisma's cost, courteously offered.

choices.label: Be the face of it
choices.outcome: The brochure is handsome and the video is better. The pledge total at the kickoff dinner is the largest the firm has seen in {diocese}. People stop you after Mass to say they gave because of you, and they mean it kindly, and each time they say it you hear the sentence the chancery will hear when you are moved: the campaign was his, and now he is gone.

effects.key: A capital campaign at his first parish was built on him personally

choices.label: Do it, on condition that {@pastor} is beside you in every photograph and at every podium
choices.outcome: The consultants dislike it and the pastor is moved by it and the brochure has two priests on it, one of them uncomfortable. The pledge total is good, not record-setting. When you are moved, the campaign has a face that stays, and the pastor, who did not want to be photographed, tells the vicar for clergy that you were the best vicar he ever had.

choices.label: Decline, and tell him why
choices.outcome: You tell him that a campaign built on a vicar is a campaign with a hole in it, and that the parish deserves one built on the parish. He is hurt and then he sees it. The firm builds it around the school families instead. It raises less. It is still there, whole, when you are gone, and that is the part of the argument you cannot prove and will not need to.

events.title: The Estimate
events.body: The parking lot at {parish} is to be repaved, and the estimate is on the rectory table waiting for {@pastor}'s signature on Thursday. It is from a contractor whose son was confirmed here, and it is eleven pages, and the pastor has read the last one. You read all of them on Tuesday night because you cannot sleep. There is something wrong with it. You are not certain what: the square footage on page three does not match the plan on page nine, or the base course is specified at a depth that seems thin for a lot that takes delivery trucks, or the subtotals do not add to the total, or all of these. It may be nothing. Contractors write bad paperwork for good work all the time. It may also be twenty thousand dollars of somebody's mistake, and the pastor is going to sign it, and it is not your parish, and the contractor's son was confirmed here, and {@maintenance} recommended him. Thursday is two days away.
events.flavorPrompt: A padded or muddled estimate that only a certain kind of past would notice. Gate the fixes on the vicar's former life.

choices.label: Read the scope the way you used to, and tell him what is padded
choices.outcome: It is the base course and the square footage both, and you have poured enough of this to know it. You mark the pages and sit with the pastor and the contractor on Thursday, and the contractor looks at you with the expression of a man who has met one of his own in a collar. The revised estimate is a good deal smaller. {@maintenance} is embarrassed and, after a week, grateful.

choices.label: Check the arithmetic, because the subtotals do not add
choices.outcome: They do not. A line has been carried twice and a percentage applied to the wrong base, and you find both in twenty minutes with a pencil. You show {@pastor} on Wednesday. He calls the contractor, who apologizes and blames his software. The corrected number is smaller by a sum the parish can feel. The pastor asks, that week, whether you would look at the school's budget too, and now you have a second job.

choices.label: Ask him to get two more bids before Thursday
choices.outcome: He says there is no time and you say you will make the calls, and you do, and two contractors from the next town come out on Wednesday with tape measures. One of them is cheaper by a margin that tells you what you needed to know. The pastor signs with the confirmation father anyway, at a revised price, because the son was confirmed here, and he is not wrong to.

choices.label: Tell him it seems high, and leave it there
choices.outcome: He says everything seems high and signs it Thursday. The lot is repaved and it is a good lot. Whether the parish paid too much for it is a thing nobody will ever know, which is how most parish money goes: not stolen, not wasted, just not looked at. You looked. You did not look hard enough to have to say so.

events.title: The Subsidy
events.body: The finance council of {parish} meets in the school library because the rectory dining room is too small for the argument. The school costs the parish a subsidy every year that is larger than every other line but salaries, and the subsidy has grown for five years while enrollment has fallen, and the council member who runs a hardware store has the spreadsheet on a projector. On one side: the principal, the school families, {@dre}, who is not a school person but knows what happens to a parish's children when the school closes, and the memory of the parish's founders, who built the school first. On the other: the hardware man, two retirees, the collection, and the arithmetic. {@pastor} presides and does not vote and has told you privately that he does not know what he thinks. He has also told you that the council will ask the vicar, because vicars are young and the school is about the young, and that you should have an answer. The projector hums. The hardware man asks what Father thinks.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish school subsidy fight in a school library. Everyone in the room is right about something.

choices.label: Argue for the school, and say that the parish will not be a parish without it
choices.outcome: You say it well, with the founders and the children and the families who moved here for it, and the room is moved, and the subsidy passes at the full number. The hardware man shakes your hand and says he hopes you are right. The collection has to carry it. {@dre} looks at you with a new respect, and the retirees, who gave the founders their money, look at the floor.

choices.label: Propose a cap on the subsidy and a three-year plan to reach it
choices.outcome: You have the numbers, and you put them beside the hardware man's, and you propose a cap that hurts and a plan that could work: enrollment targets, a tuition assistance appeal, a review each June. The council votes for it because it is a plan and they have not had one. The principal does not speak to you for a month. {@pastor} says it was the first useful thing said in that room in five years.

choices.label: Say the school is the pastor's and the council's, and that the vicar's job is to teach the children who are in it
choices.outcome: It is true and it is a dodge, and both are noted. The council argues another hour and passes the subsidy at a compromise number nobody likes. {@pastor} is grateful you did not make it harder, and slightly disappointed you did not make it easier. The children get the same religion class either way.

choices.label: Point them to the diocesan tuition assistance fund, which nobody at this table has applied to
choices.outcome: You read the diocesan financial report in the spring and remembered the fund. The hardware man had not heard of it. The application is long and you do most of it, and the grant is smaller than the gap and larger than nothing. The schools office at the chancery learns that {parish} has a vicar who reads reports, and that goes in a file with the other useful things.

events.title: The Assessment
events.body: The letter from the diocesan finance office is addressed to the pastor and {@secretary} hands it to you because {@pastor} is at a funeral and she has learned to open the ones with the finance office's return address in company. It is the annual assessment: the parish's share of the cost of running {diocese}, calculated as a percentage of ordinary income by a formula on the second page, due in twelve monthly payments, non-negotiable, and up from last year by a percentage that she reads aloud twice. The letter thanks the parish for its partnership in the mission of the Church. The secretary says the pastor will say a word she will not repeat and then pay it, as he has every year, and that the parish next door has been in arrears for three years and nobody has come for them. It is not your money and it is not your problem. It is on the desk in front of you with a paper clip.
events.flavorPrompt: The diocesan tax arrives. A vicar with a letter he was not meant to open.

choices.label: Put it in the pastor's tray
choices.outcome: He finds it after the funeral and says the word and signs the first payment. You learn what the assessment is, which you had heard of and never seen, and you learn what the pastor's face does when he sees it. That is the whole of it. The diocese is paid.

choices.label: Read the second page and check the formula against the parish's own report
choices.outcome: The finance office has counted a bequest as ordinary income, and it is not, and the letter's own formula says so. You draft a two-line note for the pastor to sign. The finance office corrects it without apology in three weeks. The difference is not large. {@pastor} says it is the first time in twenty years anyone has read page two, and means it as a compliment, mostly.

choices.label: Call the finance office and ask what the increase is for
choices.outcome: A layman with a tired voice tells you: insurance, the retired priests' fund, the seminary, the settlements. He is precise and unembarrassed. You know more about {diocese} than you did, and the finance office knows the vicar at {parish} called about the assessment, which in that building is a small, permanent note.

choices.label: Bring the percentage to the deanery and see who else got it
choices.outcome: Everyone got it. The deanery spends twenty minutes on it and a pastor of thirty years says a word the dean does not write down. It is good to have been the one who raised it; priests remember who gives them a grievance to share. The dean's report says the deanery discussed the assessment, and the vicar general knows which vicar started that.

events.title: The Count Sheets
events.body: {@parishioner} counts the collection on Sunday mornings with two others in the room behind the sacristy, and has for nineteen years, and she waits for you after the 10:30 with a folder. The count sheets do not match the deposits. Not by much: a few hundred dollars, three weeks running, always the cash. She told {@secretary} in March and was told it was a bank error. She has the bank slips. She has not told {@pastor} because, she says, the pastor does not listen to counters, and she is telling you because you listened to her about the lector schedule. She does not say who she thinks it is. She does not have to; there are only four people between the count room and the bank. You are holding the folder in the sacristy with your alb still on. You are a vicar in someone else's parish, and the person she has not named has worked here longer than the pastor, and the diocese has an internal audit office with a phone number that every parish knows and none of them calls.
events.flavorPrompt: A counter with a folder. Money missing from a parish account. The vicar is the only one who has been told.

choices.label: Take the folder to {@pastor} tonight
choices.outcome: He looks at the slips for a long time and then says he has wondered. He says he will handle it, which is a sentence you have learned to hear as a door closing. Nothing visible changes for a month. He is grateful to you in a way that does not show, and something has started in the rectory that is not finished.

choices.label: Call the diocesan internal audit office on Monday
choices.outcome: The office thanks you, asks for the slips, and says nothing about what happens next, which is their procedure. An auditor arrives at {parish} in three weeks and {@pastor} learns from her, not from you, that a vicar called. He does not shout. He says a pastor should hear it from his own house first, and he is right, and you were also right, and the two facts sit at breakfast between you.

choices.label: Ask her for the last year of sheets and go through them yourself
choices.outcome: It takes two evenings and a pot of coffee. It is not three weeks; it is fourteen months, small and regular, and it is a pattern a person made. You write it up on two pages with the dates. You have not yet decided who to hand it to. You have a document now, and in a parish a document is a thing that cannot be unwritten.

choices.label: Thank her, keep the folder, and do nothing yet
choices.outcome: You put the folder in your desk under the breviary. She asks you about it once, in the parking lot, and you say you are looking into it, and she nods in the way counters nod. The cash keeps going somewhere. You have decided that it is not yours to decide, which is a decision, and you know it.

events.title: The Auditor's Questions
events.body: It comes out the way these things do: not through you. A bank calls the chancery about an account at {parish} that the chancery did not know existed, and the diocesan auditor is in the rectory office by Thursday with a laptop and a manner that is courteous and not friendly. The person who was taking the cash is on leave by Friday and gone by the following week, and the amount, when it is finally counted, is larger than the count sheets showed and smaller than the rumor. The parish will get a letter. The diocese will not press charges, because the diocese never does, and the person will pay some of it back, and the counters will be trained again. Now the auditor wants to see you. She has the file and the timeline, and she asks the question auditors ask, which is who knew, and when, and what they did. {@pastor} is in the next room. {@parishioner}, who brought you the folder, has already been interviewed and has been exact. The auditor waits with her pen up.
events.flavorPrompt: The audit. Everyone's earlier choice is now a line in a timeline. Unsentimental.

choices.label: Say as little as you can truthfully say
choices.outcome: You answer what she asks and volunteer nothing, which is what {@pastor} did and what most priests of {diocese} would have done. The report names you as having been informed. It does not say what you did, because there was not much to say. The chancery reads it and moves on. The counters remember more than the chancery does.

choices.label: Tell her what you told {@pastor}, and when, and let him say what he did with it
choices.outcome: You give her the date. She goes to the next room. The pastor, it turns out, had called the finance office himself, quietly, a week after you spoke, and the two calls now sit in the timeline as a parish that reported itself. He comes out of the office afterward and puts a hand on your shoulder in the hallway, which he has never done.

choices.label: Tell her you called the audit office in the spring, and give her the date
choices.outcome: She has the call logged already; she wanted to see whether you would say so. You do. The report credits the vicar at {parish} with the first report and the chancery remembers it. The presbyterate hears a different version: that a vicar called the chancery on his own house, and priests have a long memory for that even when it was right.

choices.label: Hand her the two pages you wrote, with the dates
