choices.outcome: She reads them in silence and asks who taught you to do this. Your fourteen months become the spine of her report; she had six weeks. The recovery is larger because of it. The finance office asks, later, whether you would be willing to help with a parish across the diocese, and you understand that you have just been discovered by the wrong department.

choices.label: Tell her you were given a folder in the spring and put it in a drawer
choices.outcome: You say it plainly, with the date. She writes it down without expression. The report says a member of the clergy was informed and did not act, and the vicar for clergy reads that sentence and has a conversation with you that is short and not unkind and that you will remember longer than the money. {@parishioner} does not look at you at the count for a long time.

effects.key: Was told of missing parish funds and did not act

events.title: The Reporter
events.body: The city cleared the encampment under the bridge on Friday, and on Sunday your homily had one sentence about it: that a city that moves its poor out of sight has not solved anything, only its own view. It was one sentence in nine minutes on the Gospel. Somebody in the noon Mass posted the sentence, and by Monday morning a reporter from the city paper is on the rectory phone, polite and quick, asking whether Father would like to expand on his remarks about the mayor's encampment policy. {@secretary} has her hand over the receiver. {@pastor} has been in the paper once, about a school closing, and says the paper is a machine that turns a priest's sentence into a headline and the headline into a call from the chancery. The diocesan communications office has a policy, which is that priests refer press calls to the office. The reporter has a deadline of four. She says, when you take the phone, that she has already spoken to the mayor's office and they described your homily as unhelpful.
events.flavorPrompt: A single sentence from a homily becomes a press call. The register of a priest discovering what public means.

choices.label: Give her a quote that says what you said, and more
choices.outcome: You talk for eight minutes and she uses forty words, and they are the right forty. The story runs on the third page with your name and {parish} in it. The chancery calls Tuesday to remind you of the policy. The people at the shelter board call Wednesday to ask whether you would speak at their dinner. You are, in a modest way, on the record now, and the record does not have an eraser.

choices.label: Refer her to the diocesan communications office, as the policy says
choices.outcome: She sighs, audibly, and thanks you. The communications office gives her a sentence about the Church's concern for the vulnerable that she does not use. The story runs without you. The chancery notes that the vicar at {parish} followed the policy, which is a note, and the people who posted your sentence wonder why you would not say it twice.

choices.label: Tell her the sentence was taken out of context and you have no comment on the mayor
choices.outcome: It was not out of context. She knows it and prints your denial anyway, beside the sentence, and the two do not sit well together. The chancery is satisfied. The people who heard you Sunday and read you Tuesday have learned something about you they did not want to know, and one of them says so, kindly, at the door.

choices.label: Give her one sentence, on the record, exact, and smaller than what she wants
choices.outcome: You have read enough of the paper to know what it does with adjectives, and you give her a sentence with none: what the Church teaches about the poor, and that you said so. She prints it whole because there is nothing to cut. The chancery reads it and finds nothing to call about. It is the smallest possible public statement, and it is yours, and it holds.

events.title: The Invocation
events.body: The city council rotates its opening prayer among the clergy of the town, and this month the clerk's letter comes to {parish} and {@pastor} hands it to you, because he did it last year and the year before and because the council meets on Tuesday evenings during his program. The invocation is ninety seconds. The council chamber holds forty and there will be twelve, plus the councillors, the clerk, and a reporter from the weekly who is there for the zoning item. The zoning item is the shelter: a church two blocks from {parish} wants to run a winter overnight program and the neighbors have organized. It will be voted on directly after your prayer. The clerk's letter asks that the invocation be brief and non-sectarian, and the pastor says that this is a request, not a rule, and that the Baptist minister last spring prayed for four minutes in the name of Jesus and nobody stopped him. It is a small thing. The pastor says everything about the town is a small thing until it is not.
events.flavorPrompt: A ninety-second prayer before a zoning vote. Public life at municipal scale.

choices.label: Pray a plain prayer for the city and its councillors, and sit down
choices.outcome: Ninety seconds; the clerk thanks you; the vote on the shelter goes the way it was going to go. The weekly runs a photograph of the shelter's supporters and does not mention the prayer. You have done a civic thing adequately and the town has one more priest it can picture, which is what the pastor intended.

choices.label: Pray, in a line the council cannot miss, for those who will sleep outside tonight
choices.outcome: It is one sentence and it is within the prayer and it lands. Two councillors look up. The vote is the same as it was going to be, but the weekly quotes the sentence, and the neighbors who organized against the shelter, some of whom sit in the 9:00 at {parish}, know exactly whose prayer it was. The chancery reads the weekly. It reads everything.

choices.label: Pray briefly, and end it as a Catholic priest ends a prayer, whatever the clerk's letter asked
choices.outcome: You end in the name of Jesus Christ, with the sign of the cross, and one councillor crosses herself and another looks at the clerk. Nobody stops you. The weekly does not mention it. The people at {parish} who noticed, and some drove over to notice, are pleased in a way they will tell you about, and the clerk's next letter is a little cooler.

choices.label: Send the clerk a note that {parish} cannot provide a priest this month
choices.outcome: The Methodists take the slot. {@pastor} asks why and you tell him it was the zoning vote, and he says that is a reason to go, not to stay home, and he is not wrong. The town does not notice. The rectory does.

events.title: The Panel
events.body: The university's chaplaincy is hosting a panel on religion and public life, and they have asked for a Catholic priest who can hold his own beside a rabbi, an imam, and a professor of religious studies who has written a book about all three. They asked the chancery for a name and the chancery gave them yours, which is what it means to have a reputation for reading. The event is on a Thursday evening in a lecture hall; there will be a hundred people, a moderator with cards, and a question period. {@pastor} is pleased for you and says, in the same breath, that the people at {parish} do not need a priest who is good on panels, they need one who is at the hospital on Thursday evenings, and that he has heard the phrase academic, not a pastor applied to better men than either of you. The moderator has sent the questions in advance. The last one is about women's ordination. It is always about women's ordination.
events.flavorPrompt: The knowledgeable vicar is sent to a university panel. High Knowledge's cost: he is starting to be the priest who is good on panels.

choices.label: Do the panel, and keep every answer general enough to carry no weight
choices.outcome: You are good: precise, warm, and unquotable. The rabbi likes you. The professor thinks you are hiding something and says so, charmingly. The chaplaincy invites you back. The chancery hears you were credible and notes it. The people at {parish} hear you were at the university on Thursday and note that too, in a different ledger.

choices.label: Answer the last question fully: the teaching, and why you hold it
choices.outcome: You give it four minutes, with the documents and the argument from the sacraments, and you do not apologize for it. The hall is quiet in the way a hall is quiet when it disagrees and cannot say you were sloppy. The imam nods. The student paper quotes you accurately and unfavorably. Some priests of {diocese} are glad one of them said it in public. Others wish you had been at the hospital.

choices.label: Explain the teaching, and say the question deserves a better hearing than it gets
choices.outcome: You give the teaching accurately, and then you say what you think about how the Church talks about it, which is more than a priest usually says in a lecture hall with a reporter. The applause is real and it is the wrong applause for your career. The chancery calls, not angrily, to ask for the transcript. The people who follow such things in {diocese} now have a name they did not have.

choices.label: Decline, and be at the hospital on Thursday
choices.outcome: The chancery gives the chaplaincy another name. You are at the hospital, where a man on the fourth floor dies at nine with you in the room, which is not a thing that appears on any panel. {@pastor} says nothing about it, which from him is a great deal. The university does not ask again. Some of the priests who heard you were asked wonder why you said no, and one of them thinks less of you for it.

events.title: The Column
events.body: You write a column for the bulletin most weeks, four hundred words, and {@dre} posts it to the parish page on Facebook on Monday mornings because it gets more reach than the bulletin does. This week's was about the new diocesan marriage preparation policy. It was fair. It was also, in one paragraph you rewrote three times, plain about what the policy will do to the couples who come to {parish} from two towns over because their own parish turned them away, and it used the word chancery in a sentence that, when you read it on a screen at Monday noon with two hundred shares, does not read as fair. It reads as a vicar criticizing the diocese in public. A priest you have never met has commented approvingly. A layman from the marriage tribunal has commented at length. {@pastor} has seen it because {@secretary} showed him, and he has not said anything yet, which is a thing he does when he is deciding whether it is his problem. It is still up. It has been screenshotted, so in one sense it does not matter whether it stays up. In another sense it matters a great deal.
events.flavorPrompt: A bulletin column that read differently on Facebook. The public record acquiring a new entry in real time.

choices.label: Leave it up, and reply to the tribunal layman by name
choices.outcome: You answer him courteously and precisely and the thread grows. By Wednesday it is the most-read thing the parish page has ever posted. The chancellor's office sends the pastor an email with the phrase public communications policy in it. You have said what you think in a place that keeps it, and some priests are proud of you, and the chancery has a screenshot with a date.

choices.label: Ask {@dre} to take it down
choices.outcome: She does, at once, with a look. The screenshots circulate anyway, now with the added information that it was removed, which reads as a retraction or a silencing depending on who is reading. The chancery is satisfied. The two hundred people who shared it are not. You learn that a thing taken down is a second thing, not the absence of the first.

choices.label: Edit the paragraph and post a note saying you did and why
choices.outcome: You rewrite the paragraph to say exactly what you meant and post a two-line note above it saying the earlier version was unclear about the diocese's role. It is true. It is also a small, honorable retreat, and it is read as one by everyone, and the tribunal layman replies to say he appreciates it. The chancery notices the note and decides you are manageable.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} it is his page and his call
choices.outcome: He is relieved to be asked and leaves it up, because taking it down would be a story, and he tells the chancellor's office so himself. It is the first time he has defended you to the diocese and he does it without telling you. The column stays. Your name is on it, and his is now beside it in a file, and he knows that, and did it anyway.

events.title: Forty Days
events.body: The parish Respect Life committee has kept a vigil outside the clinic on the state road every Lent for eleven years: two hours on Saturday mornings, a rosary, signs the diocese approved, a thermos. {@parishioner} chairs it and asks you, after the Friday Stations, whether you would come and lead the rosary this Saturday, because {@pastor} never has, in eleven years, and the committee has stopped asking him. She says it without bitterness. She says a priest at the vigil changes it: the people driving past see a collar, and the clinic staff see a collar, and the newspaper, which sends a photographer once a Lent, sees a collar. That is the point and that is the problem. The pastor, when you mention it, says he has stayed away not because he disagrees but because a pastor who is photographed at the clinic is a pastor who has chosen which half of his parish he belongs to, and that a vicar has the same choice and less standing. The committee will be there at nine with or without you. The photographer comes when he comes.
events.flavorPrompt: A Lenten vigil outside a clinic; a collar changes what it means. The pastor's reasoning is practical, not cowardly.

choices.label: Go, and lead the rosary
choices.outcome: There are fourteen of them and it is cold. You lead the Sorrowful Mysteries and the photographer comes at ten and the photograph runs Monday with your collar in it and the parish's name in the caption. The committee is moved. The people at {parish} who have never mentioned the clinic mention it now, on both sides. You have been seen, which was the point, and it was.

choices.label: Go, lead the rosary, and say at the end that the parish will also be at the shelter and the crisis pregnancy center this Lent
choices.outcome: You lead the rosary and then you say the other sentence, about the mother and the child and the rent, and the committee hears it as an addition and the photographer misses it entirely. The photograph is the same photograph. But the committee starts collecting diapers the following week, and two of the people who never mention the clinic help, and the parish is a little less divided than the pastor feared.

choices.label: Go, but stand at the back without a stole and let {@parishioner} lead
choices.outcome: You are there and you are not the point. The photographer photographs the signs. The committee is glad and slightly puzzled. The pastor says that was a vicar's answer and means it as praise. It is a small thing, done quietly, on a cold morning, and nobody who was not there knows.

choices.label: Decline, and tell her the parish should be at the shelter on Wednesdays before it is at the clinic on Saturdays
choices.outcome: She hears you out and does not agree and does not argue; she has heard it before from priests. The committee goes without you. Word of what you said reaches the Wednesday people, who are pleased, and the Saturday people, who are not, and both groups are the parish. The pastor says you chose a half after all, and that it was the other one.

events.title: Sunday's Paper
events.body: It is on the front page of the Sunday paper below the fold, and by the 7:30 half the church has read it. A man of forty-one, named, with his photograph, says that a priest assigned to {parish} in the years he was an altar server abused him for two years, and that he told a priest at the time, and that nothing happened. The accused is dead. The diocese's statement, which the reporter quotes in full, says that it received the allegation in the spring, found it credible, and has reached out to the survivor; it does not say why the parish was not told. {@pastor} was not here then. He read the paper at six and said the 7:30 with a face like a wall and has said nothing to you. The chancery's email arrived at eight: pastors are to read the diocesan statement at all Masses; no further comment. The 10:30 is yours. The people are quieter than usual coming in, and some of them are the age of the man in the photograph, and some of them were altar servers here, and all of them are looking at the ambo.
events.flavorPrompt: An allegation against a predecessor surfaces in the paper. The vicar has the 10:30. Grave, exact, no melodrama.

choices.label: Read the statement, and then speak to them from the ambo in your own words
choices.outcome: You say that this happened in this building, that the man in the paper was one of ours, that the people who did not act were also ours, and that the parish will not pretend otherwise. You do not say more than you know. There is a silence afterward that is not the usual silence. The chancery wanted the statement read. Two people wait for you afterward and one of them cannot speak.

choices.label: Read the diocesan statement exactly as sent and go on with the Mass
choices.outcome: You read it. It takes forty seconds and the paragraph about reaching out to the survivor sounds, in your mouth, like what it is. The Mass continues. Nobody waits for you afterward, and you learn later that several people wanted to and did not, because the reading told them there was nothing to say. The chancery is satisfied with {parish}.

choices.label: Call the communications office before the 10:30 and ask what they know that the statement does not say
choices.outcome: The duty officer tells you more than the statement did: the date the allegation came in, the review board's finding, the reason the parish was not told, which is a bad reason and a real one. You read the statement at the 10:30 and add two true sentences the office cleared. It is better than the statement and worse than the truth, and it is what the diocese will let a vicar say.

choices.label: Before the 10:30, ask {@pastor}, with the door shut, what he knows
choices.outcome: He knows more than the paper. He was a young priest in {diocese} when the man in the photograph was an altar server, and he knew the accused, and he says he heard things at the time that he took for the things young priests hear. He has not said this to anyone. He has said it to you. You read the statement at the 10:30 with his words in your pocket, and you carry them from then on.

events.title: The List
events.body: {diocese} publishes its list on a Tuesday: every priest credibly accused of the abuse of a minor since the diocese kept records, with dates, assignments, and status, on the diocesan website and in the paper. There are more names than anyone at the deanery guessed and fewer than the survivors' group said there would be. Three of them were assigned to {parish} at some point; one of them is a name the older parishioners will recognize from a plaque in the hall. The chancery's instructions to pastors are precise: the list is to be made available in the bulletin or the vestibule; a paragraph is provided; no names are to be read aloud. {@pastor} hands you the paragraph and the list and says the bulletin is yours this week because he cannot do it, and he says it without explanation and goes to his room. {@secretary} is waiting to know what goes in. The bulletin prints Thursday. The plaque is still in the hall.
events.flavorPrompt: The diocesan list is published. The vicar does the bulletin; the pastor cannot. Institutional gravity, no sermon.

choices.label: Print the paragraph, the link, and a note of your own about the three names and the plaque
choices.outcome: You write six sentences. You name the three assignments, and you say the plaque will come down this week, and you say where a person can call. {@maintenance} takes the plaque down on Friday without being asked twice. The chancery did not ask for the note. Several people keep that bulletin, which is not a thing that happens to bulletins.

choices.label: Print the diocesan paragraph and the link, and nothing else
choices.outcome: It goes in on page three, below the anniversary Masses. The people who go looking find it. The plaque stays up until someone on the pastoral council asks about it in the spring, and then it comes down with no note at all. {parish} did what the chancery asked, and the chancery asked the minimum, and the minimum is what was done.

choices.label: Print the paragraph, and preach on the list at your Masses that Sunday
choices.outcome: You preach on it: not on the priests, on the parish, on what it means that these men said Mass at this altar. It is the hardest homily you have given. Some of the priests of {diocese}, when they hear, think it was the right thing and some think you made the parish carry something that was the chancery's to carry. The people at the door afterward are not divided.

choices.label: Put the link in the bulletin and let the website carry it
choices.outcome: A line on page four with a web address. Most people do not follow it. The plaque stays. {@pastor} does not ask what you did with the bulletin and you do not tell him, and the two of you have agreed, without saying so, that the parish's part in this was to be quiet. Some people notice the quiet. One of them says so.

events.title: Did You Know
events.body: {@parishioner} waits for you in the parking lot after the Saturday Vigil, by your car, in the dark, so that it will not be in the church. He is in his sixties. He was an altar server here. He asks whether you knew, and then, before you can answer, whether {@pastor} knew, and then, before you can answer that, why nobody said anything for thirty years, and he does not mean the diocese, he means the priests, the ones who ate at his mother's table. He is not shouting. He has been waiting to ask a priest this since the paper, and you are the priest who is standing here. Behind him the church lights go off one bank at a time as {@maintenance} locks up. You were a child when it happened. That is true and it is not an answer. He knows what the diocese has said. He wants to know what you say, in a parking lot, with nobody from the communications office listening.
events.flavorPrompt: A parishioner asks, in a dark parking lot, whether the priests knew. The vicar owes him a true sentence.

choices.label: Tell him you were a child then, that you do not know what the pastor knew, and that you will not guess
choices.outcome: You say it plainly, and you say that you are sorry, and you say it the way a man says it, not a statement. He looks at you for a while and then he nods and says that is the first straight thing a priest has said to him about it. You stand there until the last bank of lights goes off. He is at the 7:30 next week, which he had not been for a month.

choices.label: Tell him the diocese has handled it and that the review board's process is sound
choices.outcome: You say what the chancery's email said, in your own voice, and it is not a lie and it is not what he asked. He says thank you, Father, in the tone in which that phrase closes a conversation, and gets into his car. He is not at Mass the following week or the one after. The chancery would have approved of every word.

choices.label: Tell him what {@pastor} told you with the door shut
choices.outcome: You tell him: that the pastor heard things as a young priest and took them for the things young priests hear. It is the pastor's confidence and you have spent it in a parking lot on a man who was owed it. He is quiet for a long time. He says he will not repeat it, and he does not. The pastor learns you told someone; he does not know whom; he does not ask; breakfast is different afterward.

choices.label: Say nothing yet; sit with him on the bench by the door until he has said all of it
choices.outcome: It takes an hour. He tells you about the sacristy, the summer of the plaque, his mother, the priest who ate at their table, and what he did not say to anyone until he was fifty. You do not explain anything. At the end he says he did not need an answer, he needed a priest to hear it, and that you did. {@maintenance} left the vestibule light on for you.

events.title: The Dinner at the Big House
events.body: The invitation is handwritten and the house is the one with the gates. The family hosts a dinner four times a year for the priests of {diocese} who, as the invitation puts it, love the Church's tradition, and this quarter you are invited. There are nine priests at the table, two of them pastors of the largest parishes in the diocese, and a monsignor who was once close to a previous bishop, and the food is very good, and the conversation is about the seminary, the liturgy, the new bishop, and the vicar for clergy, in that order and with increasing candor. They are kind to you. They have read something you wrote or heard something you preached. Over the port the host asks whether you would consider becoming chaplain to the schola that sings the Latin Mass at the chapel across the river: an evening a week, a stipend, a community that would, he says, be devoted to you. The monsignor says the chancery does not love the schola and does not need to. The pastors say nothing, which is its own information.
events.flavorPrompt: The traditionalist bloc courts a young priest over port. Warm, intelligent, and a door that closes behind you.

choices.label: Accept the chaplaincy
choices.outcome: The schola is thirty people who sing well and love you at once, and the evening a week becomes the best evening of your week. The chancery learns of it in a month. Nothing is said. Something is written. You have a home in {diocese} now, and it is across the river, and the men at the big house speak of you as one of theirs.

choices.label: Enjoy the dinner, decline the chaplaincy gracefully, and accept the next invitation
choices.outcome: You say you are a vicar and that a vicar's evenings are his pastor's, which is true and which the monsignor accepts with a look that says he has heard it before from men who later said yes. You are invited again in the spring. You are on a list now, a pleasant one, and lists of this kind are read by both sides.

choices.label: Decline the chaplaincy, and do not go back
choices.outcome: You write a courteous note. The next invitation does not come. The men at the big house are not vindictive; they simply have a long memory and a short list. At a deanery months later one of the pastors who said nothing over the port says, in passing, that he had thought you were one of them, and moves on.

choices.label: Decline, and tell the table why you think the schola across the river is a mistake
choices.outcome: You say it over the port, respectfully, and the table goes quiet in a way that is not hostile, only final. The monsignor thanks you for your candor, a phrase the chancery also uses. You are not invited again. What you said travels, as things said at that table do, and reaches people who are glad a young priest said it, and people who will not forget that he did.

events.title: The Justice Network
events.body: The letter is from the diocesan justice and peace network, which is a body the bishop tolerates, funds a little, and does not attend. Its board has a vacancy for a priest under ten years ordained, and two of its members, a sister who ran the Catholic Worker house for twenty years and a pastor with a parish in the poorest deanery of {diocese}, take you to lunch to ask. They are direct. The network is drafting a public letter on the county's housing policy; it wants the board to sign it; it wants a young priest's name near the top because the bishop's office reads the signatures from the top. They tell you the board meets monthly, that its members are not promoted, and that they would rather you knew that now. The sister says the network is where the diocese keeps its conscience so that it does not have to carry it around. The pastor says that was unfair and then does not correct it. They do not ask for an answer over lunch. They ask for one by the end of the month, and the housing letter goes to the paper on the first.
events.flavorPrompt: The progressive bloc courts a young priest over a cheap lunch. Honest about what it costs.

choices.label: Join the board and sign the housing letter
choices.outcome: Your name is fourth on the letter and the bishop's office reads it fourth. The board is earnest, underfunded, and welcoming, and the meetings are long. The people of the poorest deanery learn your name before the chancery does, which is a kind of promotion the chancery does not track. The men at the big house across the diocese cross you off a list you did not know you were on.

choices.label: Join the board, and tell them you will not sign public letters in your first years
choices.outcome: The sister says that is a chancery answer and the pastor says it is a sensible one and they let you join on those terms. You are useful to the board in the way you are useful to everyone: you read the budget. Your name is not on the letter. The network has a priest who works and does not sign, and it has had those before, and it knows what they become.

choices.label: Decline, with thanks
choices.outcome: The sister is not surprised. The pastor is a little. They find another young priest, and the letter runs with his name fourth, and he is, a decade later, exactly where they said he would be, which is where he wanted to be. You are on no list. The chancery does not know a lunch happened.

choices.label: Decline, and tell them the network's letters are politics wearing a collar
choices.outcome: You say it at the lunch table, and the sister laughs, not warmly, and says she has been told that by bishops. The pastor pays for lunch and does not shake your hand. It travels. The people in {diocese} who think as you do hear that a young priest said it to the network's face, and the people who do not hear that too.

events.title: The Day for the Newly Ordained
events.body: Twice a year {diocese} gathers the priests ordained fewer than five years for a day at the retreat house: Morning Prayer, a speaker, lunch, a session with {@vicar_for_clergy}, Evening Prayer, and the drive home. This time the speaker is a psychologist on boundaries and burnout, and the session with the vicar for clergy is titled Your First Assignment: What We Are Learning. There are eleven of you, including {@closest_classmate} and {@rival_classmate}, and the room is the same one where you made your canonical retreat before ordination. The psychologist is good and says nothing you did not know and one thing you did not want to. Lunch is better than the seminary's. The session afterward is the reason the day exists: the vicar for clergy asks, one by one, how it is going, in front of the others, and eleven men decide in real time how much of the truth to say in a room where the man beside them will be a pastor when they are, or before.
events.flavorPrompt: A diocesan formation day for the young priests: half retreat, half evaluation, entirely observed.

choices.label: Go, and say in the session what everyone says
choices.outcome: Good pastor, good people, busy, learning a great deal. It is what the man before you said and what the man after you says. The vicar for clergy nods eleven times. You have a day away from the parish, which is worth something, and you drive home with a classmate, which is worth more.

choices.label: Go, and say one true thing in the session that the others have not
choices.outcome: You say it briefly: the thing about the parish or the pastor or yourself that is actually the case. The room changes temperature. Two men say something true after you, and the vicar for clergy writes for longer than usual. On the drive home {@closest_classmate} says you either helped everyone or ended your career, and that he could not tell which.

choices.label: Send regrets; there is a funeral
choices.outcome: There is a funeral, and {@pastor} could have taken it. The vicar for clergy's assistant sends a note asking you to confirm you will attend the next one. Your classmates have a day you did not have. The chancery has a count of who comes, because the chancery has a count of everything, and yours is one lower.

choices.label: Go, say the usual, and find {@vicar_for_clergy} at lunch to ask what the diocese is actually learning
choices.outcome: He tells you, over the soup, more than the session will: which parishes are burning men out, which pastors the diocese is watching, what the bishop said at the last personnel board. It is not confidential and it is not for everyone. He tells you because you asked well. You drive home knowing more about {diocese} than any of your classmates.

events.title: The Chrism Mass
events.body: The Chrism Mass is on Tuesday of Holy Week at the cathedral, at eleven, so that priests from the far end of {diocese} can drive in and be home for evening confessions. The presbyterate vests in the undercroft, a hundred men in white in a room that smells of coffee and old incense, and processes in by order of ordination, which puts you near the front with the men you know and far from the ones you have been hearing about. {@bishop} blesses the oils. Before that, he asks the priests to stand and renew the promises they made at ordination: to be more united to the Lord, to be faithful stewards of the mysteries, to follow Christ the Head and Shepherd, not seeking any gain. You say I am, with a hundred other men, in a cathedral, in front of the people, with the week in front of you that will take everything you have. His homily to the priests is about fatigue, and it is a good one, and it is possible he means it. Lunch afterward is in the hall: the retired men at one table, the chancery at another, the deanery cliques, the men on leave who came anyway. Confessions at {parish} are at four.
events.flavorPrompt: Holy Week's one hour of fraternity, with a renewal of promises inside it. The register is tired and true.

choices.label: Renew the promises and mean them, all of them, this year
choices.outcome: You say I am and you find, standing there, that it is true, or true enough to carry into the week. The bishop's homily lands on you in a way you had not expected. You skip nothing that afternoon. The Triduum is hard and you are in it. It will not always be like this. It is like this now.

choices.label: Renew them, and name to yourself, precisely, the one you are not sure of
choices.outcome: You say I am. You know which promise you said with a reservation, and you are honest with yourself about it standing in the cathedral, which is a more useful place to be honest than most. It does not resolve. You carry it into the week and it is heavier and it is yours. The bishop's homily on fatigue was, you decide, addressed to someone else.

choices.label: Leave after the Mass and be back at {parish} early for confessions
choices.outcome: You are in the confessional at three-thirty and there is already a line. The priests who stayed for lunch have a story about the vicar general and a fish course that you will hear secondhand for a year. {@pastor}, who stayed, says a vicar who skips the Chrism lunch will regret it later, when he needs the men in that room, and he is not wrong, and the line at the confessional is not wrong either.

choices.label: Stay for lunch and sit at the retired priests' table
choices.outcome: They are glad of a young face and they talk: about bishops you never met, parishes that no longer exist, a Chrism Mass in the year of the fire. One of them tells you which men in the room to trust and is specific. You are back at {parish} at ten past four and the line has waited. You know more about {diocese} than the vicar for clergy would ever tell you, and two old men have your name now.

events.title: The Planning Office
events.body: Two people from the diocesan office of pastoral planning arrive on a Wednesday with a laptop, a camera, and a printed map of the deanery on which {parish} is a circle with a number in it. {@pastor} is at a funeral in the next county and either did not know they were coming or did not want to be here when they came. {@secretary} has shown them into the parlor and come to find you. They are courteous and they are in a hurry: they want to see the church, the hall, the school building if there is one, the rectory, the parking, and the books, and they want to ask a few questions about Mass attendance, sacramental counts, and, as the younger one puts it, the parish's realistic prospects. The rumor has been going for a year that {parish} is on a list. The map on the table is the list. Nobody has said the word merger. The older one asks whether Father would mind walking them through the buildings and answering what he can, and whether the pastor has a view about the church two miles east, which is also a circle on the map.
events.flavorPrompt: The planning office walks the buildings while the pastor is away. The map on the table is the rumor.

choices.label: Walk them through everything and answer every question straight
choices.outcome: You show them the roof, the boiler, the hall, the empty classrooms, and you give them the counts you know. They thank you and mean it. The report they write is accurate, which is the best and the worst thing a report can be. When the rumor becomes a letter, some of the people at {parish} remember that it was the vicar who gave the chancery the tour, and the chancery remembers that too, differently.

choices.label: Show them the church and the hall on a good day, and let the counts speak for themselves
choices.outcome: You take them through the church with the afternoon light in it and past the hall while the seniors' lunch is on and you do not offer the boiler room. They are professionals and they know a tour when they get one. The report is a little kinder than the truth. The pastor, when he hears, says you did what he would have done, which is what he wanted and not quite a compliment.

choices.label: Give them coffee and tell them, courteously, that the buildings and the books are the pastor's to show
choices.outcome: They accept it; they have heard it before. They come back the following week when {@pastor} is here, and he gives them a tour that is mostly an argument, and they write it down. He is grateful to you in a way he does not say. The planning office notes that {parish} has a vicar who knows whose parish it is, which is a note with two readings.

choices.label: Walk them through, and ask to see the map properly before they leave
choices.outcome: The older one hesitates and then turns it around, because you asked as a colleague. The circles have numbers and the numbers are attendance over debt over building condition, and {parish} is not the worst circle in the deanery and is not the best. You know now what the chancery knows. The pastor does not, until you tell him, and he does not ask how you found out.
